scope: How a delivery team defines milestones, sequences the work between them, sets target dates, keeps the schedule current, checks its dependency chains for cycles and finds the critical path, and accounts for every at-risk or blocked milestone. General practice for any delivery team; projectteam's own paths, formats and specialist names are excluded, as are delivery dependencies on other teams (dependency-tracking), tasks and their blockers (task-breakdown) and the general record-linking convention (project-record-linking). Apple, Android and Windows have no bearing on this topic.
research_type: How-to / troubleshooting (intent Do; domain project scheduling; method standards bodies and practitioner sources). Product / how-to LOW-MEDIUM bar, no escalation; no metric claim is made, so the Statistical bar is not invoked.

questions.text: Best practices: what is current best practice for this topic?
Known solutions: what solutions, patterns, libraries and tools already exist, and how do they compare?
Platform guidelines: what do the platform owners' own guidelines say, for each platform the topic touches (Apple, Android, Windows, web, the databases and runtimes concerned)?
The expert's view: if we hired an expert consultant in this topic, what would they tell us: what to do, what to avoid, and what people usually get wrong?

research_questions: Best practice: how should a team set milestones, sequence the work between them, set target dates and keep the schedule current?

Known solutions: how do milestone plans, roadmaps, Gantt charts, critical path method and rolling-wave planning compare for a software team, and which do GitHub milestones, Jira and Linear cycles support?
Platform guidelines: what do the PMBOK Guide's schedule guidance, ISO 21502 and the Scrum and Kanban Guides say about milestones, dates and forecasting?
The expert's view: what do delivery leads say teams get wrong with schedules (dates without dependencies, no buffer, milestones blocked with no reason recorded), and what to do instead?

Milestone cycle detection: find how scheduling practice and tools detect cycles in a dependency chain and find the critical path, and state how a milestone plan is checked so its chains hold no cycle.

Blocked milestone accounting: find how practitioners tie a milestone's status to the risks and issues that explain it, and state the rule that every blocked or at-risk milestone names the issue or risk that blocks it.

methodology.method: guidelines/researching/process/research-methodology-and-sources: orient and classify (project scheduling; how-to), go to the authoritative sources for the domain (a government audit standard for schedules, the method owners' guides, the issue trackers' own documentation, the runtime library docs for graph checks), chain citations, corroborate across independent publishers, record provenance at generation time.
methodology.search_strategy: WebSearch for each research question against standards bodies (GAO, ISO, PMI, APM, AXELOS/PeopleCert), method owners (Scrum Guide, Kanban Guide, Scaled Agile), the trackers (GitHub Docs, Atlassian Support, Linear Docs), scheduling tools and libraries (Microsoft Project, Python graphlib, NetworkX) and named practitioners (Construx/McConnell, Spolsky, Basecamp Shape Up); WebFetch of every cited page; the GAO guide and the Construx white paper read in full as text extracted from their PDFs with pdftotext, and every quote from them taken from that text.
methodology.inclusion: Primary sources first: GAO-16-89G, the Scrum Guide, the Kanban Guide, Scaled Agile's own framework pages, PeopleCert's PRINCE2 7 article, APM's own pages, the trackers' and tools' own documentation. Named-expert secondary sources (McConnell, Spolsky, Singer) only for the expert's-view and comparison questions no primary source covers.
methodology.exclusion: Search-result snippets, training-provider and exam-prep summaries of PRINCE2 and PMBOK, template vendors' blog posts (Miro, Lucid, Aha!, Smartsheet), community forum answers, pages that refused the fetch (PMI, ISO OBP, gaoinnovations.gov HTML, ANSI previews, GovS 002 download) and any quote not found in the fetched page.
methodology.scoring: guidelines/researching/evidence/verification-and-trust-scoring: Authority 30 + Independent corroboration 25 + Accuracy/verifiability 20 + Currency 10 + Transparency 15, capped by the Product / how-to LOW-MEDIUM domain bar (broad independent consensus); a vendor's documentation of its own product is scored as authoritative for that product only.

summary: Three of the five rules hold at their stated strength: defining and sequencing milestones with target dates, dependency chains and status (GAO-16-89G Best Practice 2, GitHub milestones, Linear milestones and project dependencies, Jira plan dependencies, SAFe's planning board); identifying at-risk and blocked milestones (GitHub and Linear status updates, Jira off-track warnings and flags, the Kanban and Scrum Guides on impediments); and chains having no cycles, which is a logical necessity: GAO says an activity cannot have its successor also be its predecessor, Microsoft Project cannot calculate dates across a circular dependency, and a topological order exists if and only if the graph is acyclic (Python graphlib, which reports the cycle). Two rules are unsupported at the must-hold strength their Verify wording carries: 'every milestone has a status and target date' and 'no milestone is blocked without a corresponding issue or concern' are supported only as SHOULD (GAO's schedule narrative should report key milestone status and explain date changes; Linear and GitHub make milestone dates optional; Jira's flag comment and Linear's update text are optional). The research adds eleven practices no rule covers: milestones as zero-duration key events, logic links over fixed dates, a topological-sort cycle check, the critical path as the longest path, statusing against a status date, explicit schedule contingency, a baseline with variance, a narrative explaining every date change, naming the risk behind an at-risk milestone, forecasting dates from history as ranges, and (MAY) fixing the date while flexing scope, or committing the near term while forecasting the rest.
open_questions: Whether the two unsupported Verify rules (milestone-has-status-and-target-date, blocked-milestone-has-issue-or-concern) are kept as must-hold checks by house policy or restated at the SHOULD strength the sources support; the owner decides.

Whether 'target date' in milestone-has-status-and-target-date means a fixed committed date or a forecast computed from logic: GAO says baseline and status schedules should not carry hard date constraints, so a policy that every milestone carries a fixed date conflicts with logic-driven scheduling unless the date is a baseline target.

Whether the at-risk case joins the blocked case in one rule (every blocked or at-risk milestone names its issue or risk) or stays a separate rule; the brief's research question asks for both, the listed rule names only blocked.

Which status vocabulary the cookbook names: Linear uses On track / At risk / Off track, GitHub Projects uses On track / At risk among others, Jira uses a Flagged = Impediment field; the owner decides whether to fix a vocabulary or leave it to the tracker.

Whether the cookbook names a schedule update cadence; GAO ties cadence to duration, complexity and risk and gives only an example (track weekly when reporting monthly), so any fixed cadence is a policy choice.

Whether 'fix the date, flex the scope' (Shape Up, Scrum's fixed-length Sprint) is stated as an option beside critical-path scheduling or left out; the sources present it as a method choice, not a universal practice.
limitations: PMI's own pages (the PMBOK Guide, the Practice Standard for Scheduling, PMI Learning Library papers on critical path and rolling-wave planning) returned HTTP 403 to every fetch, and the ANSI preview of the Practice Standard for Scheduling did too; no PMI wording is quoted, and the PMBOK Guide's schedule guidance is not established here.

ISO 21502:2020 is paywalled and its iso.org page and OBP preview refused the fetch; only ISO TC 258's public scope summary was read, which says nothing about schedules or milestones, so no ISO 21502 claim on scheduling is made. ISO 31000 was not reached.

No AXELOS/PeopleCert primary text on PRINCE2 7's Plans or Progress practices (tolerances, exception reports, highlight reports) could be fetched; the AXELOS progress blog returned only its page title. PRINCE2 is represented only by PeopleCert's article on the Issues practice.
LeSS was not researched; no LeSS page on milestones or dates was reached in the time available.
The UK GovS 002 project delivery standard download refused the fetch; no UK government text is quoted.

Linear's issue-relations page returned 404; Linear's blocking behaviour is cited from its project-dependencies page only. No tracker page was found saying whether GitHub, Linear or Jira refuse to create a cyclic dependency at entry time; Jira's own KB treats cycles as something to detect afterwards.

The Construx cone-of-uncertainty figures (4x to 0.25x) rest on research the white paper does not name, sample or measure; they are not used as a claim, only McConnell's qualitative advice on commitments is.
Apple, Android and Windows platform guidelines have no bearing on milestone scheduling and were not researched.
